Puzzle by Alexander Bogomolny (cut-the-knot.org)

Game: Draw bridges between the tall lines, then follow each line from the top to see where it comes out.
How to play: Drag from one line to another to draw a bridge. Choose Verify, then click each line to follow it down.
Look for the math

This puzzle comes from Martin Gardner's Mathematical Games column (Scientific American, December 1959). Draw as many shuttles as you like, in any places: when you follow the lines from the top, two different lines never come out at the same bottom. The logic test for this page checked that claim for every arrangement of up to three shuttle heights on 2 to 5 lines, and it always holds.

Walking the lines

Start at the top of a line and go down. Whenever you meet the end of a shuttle, cross it to the other line and keep going down. The path you trace is called an itinerary. In Verify mode the applet draws each itinerary and writes the starting number at the bottom it reaches, so you can read off where every line ends up. A line cannot hold two shuttles at exactly the same height — the applet refuses with “This location is occupied! Select another.”

Every shuttle is a swap

Imagine each line carrying its own number downwards. Read the shuttles from top to bottom: each one exchanges the numbers on the two lines it joins, and leaves all the others alone. Such a swap of two things is called a transposition, and the final arrangement of numbers is a permutation of the starting one: doing several swaps in a row, one after another, is the product of those transpositions. Every permutation can be built this way.

Why two lines never meet

Think of the lines as ropes and each shuttle as a place where two ropes cross. Ropes can cross but they cannot merge, so the number of rope ends at the bottom equals the number at the top. One shuttle keeps the matching between tops and bottoms one-to-one — a bijection — and adding one more shuttle keeps it one-to-one again. By induction, any number of shuttles does: different tops always reach different bottoms. That is also why the puzzle can share out jobs or snacks fairly: everybody's line ends somewhere, and nobody shares a bottom.

Two walks through every shuttle

The original page ends with a question: prove that every shuttle is used by exactly two itineraries, one crossing it left to right and one right to left. The logic test counted crossings on all those boards and confirmed it. Here is one way to see it: stand at one end of a shuttle and walk backwards (upwards, crossing shuttles in reverse) until you reach a top — that top's itinerary crosses the shuttle in one direction. Do the same from the other end, and you get a second, different top crossing it the other way. No third walk can use the shuttle, because a walk meets it only by coming down one of its two lines, and each line delivers exactly one walk to that height.

Try to send line 1 all the way to the last bottom using as few shuttles as possible — then predict where every other line ends before you press Verify.
